payload.text: For the past few decades, the vast majority of U.S. startup funding has consistently gone to companies in blue states or purple states, where Democrats control all or some statewide offices. But with Tuesday’s election results, the investment divide between blue, purple and red states has grown even more pronounced. So far this year, less than 2% of all startup investment has gone to companies in post-election red states, defined as those that will have both a Republican governor and two Republican U.S. senators. The red states’ share is much smaller than in years’ past due to five states shifting to purple. Of those, the largest venture hub is Texas, which shifted to purple with the election of Democratic Senator James Talarico and Governor Gina Hinojosa, followed by Ohio. This year, as of Election Day, startups in the remaining 17 red states 1 , which are home to nearly a quarter of Americans, had collectively pulled in just $8.6 billion in venture funding, with Florida, Tennessee and Utah among the largest contributors. To put that in perspective: It’s less than the typical nationwide total in a single week. Purple states rising The 10 purple U.S. states 2 , meanwhile, are home to just over a quarter of Americans and pulled in about $28.6 billion this year as of Election Day. That’s much higher than the red state tally, but still less than 6% of all U.S. startup funding. Beyond the aforementioned newcomers Texas and Ohio, several other purple states regularly pull in sizable venture funding, including Pennsylvania, North Carolina and to some extent Wisconsin. Also worth noting: The divide between red, purple and blue states is somewhat less stark when it comes to round counts. About 12% of startup financings of $1 million or more went to purple state companies this year, and about 9% went to red states. Broadly, it looks like backers are still finding plenty of investment-worthy talent outside of blue states when it comes to smaller deals. However, they are concentrating most of their capital into big AI rounds for California and New York companies. Blue states get over 90% of startup funding This brings us to our next point: Blue states receive the overwhelming majority of startup funding, of which most goes to California. 3 Per a Crunchbase analysis last week, California companies had pulled in more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding in 2026. Most of that stems from mega-financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic . While no other state comes close to California for attracting investment, the nearest runners up are also predominantly blue states, including New York and Massachusetts. In total, blue states have pulled in a staggering $481 billion in startup investment this year as of Election Day, per Crunchbase data, a new record. Politics and what makes for a venture hub So is it politics, or coincidence? Broadly speaking, the qualities that geographic startup hubs share — such as a deep tech talent pool, urban environs, leading tech companies and top research universities — aren’t specifically the domain of blue states. That said, predominantly rural states, which tend to lean red, are less likely to have those ingredients. Even so, there’s no rule against red state startup prowess. Austin, for example, managed to cement its status as a major tech hub even while Texas remained solidly under Republican control. And Utah also boasts a sophisticated startup scene. But following a Democratic electoral sweep, it’s hardly a surprise that more startup hubs now find themselves located in blue or purple states. payload.text: The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires. This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI (now part of SpaceX ), Anduril Industries , Databricks , Prometheus and The Boring Co. These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data. Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally  well-off to boot. The world’s wealthiest men Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos . Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself. Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion. AI’s leading names The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth. OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit . Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman , by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year. At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei . Databricks, Anduril and others Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures. Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth , with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing. Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf , meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey , who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth. Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore , Figure founder Brett Adcock , and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen , among others. Billionaire categories We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments. Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale. Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions. Updating the venture archetype But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well. True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types. Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires. payload.text: Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion. The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding. Funding concentration Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital , Index Ventures and Lux Capital . DeepSeek ’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance , and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI . DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI , a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board . The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity. Other large rounds last month went to Axiom , which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp , which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent , which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi , which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes , which raised a $1 billion Series A. AI-driven A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI , which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev. A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month. Exits The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX ’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion . On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber ’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion. Looking ahead With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds. The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026. Cohere is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October, without reporting an initial or final close . This funding was not included in the October monthly totals. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. Glossary of funding terms Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round. Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.) Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3. Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups. Large rounds dominate funding One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more. As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023. The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic . But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds. Deals keep falling even as dollars rise In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared. In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year. The early-stage slump Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low. It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups , with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips. Looking ahead Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom. A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure. But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars. payload.text: Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo , which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital , Isai and Ternel . The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments. Exits Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities. Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets , a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February. On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November. Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing. payload.text: More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots. Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1 , the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low. Smaller Series B rounds grow scarcer One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds. So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data. The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set. Big rounds still a big thing On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular. At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals. Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus , Jeff Bezos ’ physical AI startup that launched last year. Model developer World Labs , led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li , was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor. For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients. Mostly an AI story Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group. So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories. AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies. Bullish climate for Series B Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed. Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies. payload.text: Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning. U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done. Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase . Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020. Size your seed against the Series A Uncork Capital ‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal. A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic , a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed , right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures , then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later. Map your Series A leads now Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything. Sell your way to the bar The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion. At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine. From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside. A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one. As the co-founder and managing partner of MGV , Marc Schröder is committed to establishing MGV as the premier venture firm for world-class tech entrepreneurs to accelerate their visions. Under Schröder’s stewardship, MGV has swiftly ascended to a top-quartile firm, surpassing the performance of 95% of venture funds. Business Insider has recognized him as one of the Top 100 global seed investors , and his perspectives are published regularly in Crunchbase News and other leading publications. payload.text: Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels. Rebekah Johnson, founder and CEO of Numericle. (Courtesy photo) The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation. The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected. Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents. Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers. For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning. Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone. From a regulatory warning to a company Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West , said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission ’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016. She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling. About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen. “Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking. Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle. She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes. “When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said. That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A. Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare. The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers. Verifying increasingly convincing fakes Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls. Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers. A business call from Numeracle, delivered with name, logo, and reason for calling. (Photo courtesy of Numeracle) Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam. AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles. “The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.” She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail. Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort. The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call. Investor POV: ‘Doing more with less’ For Lenard Marcus , a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers. He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.” Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales. Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said. “She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added. Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent. “This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said. title: Chronosphere
summary: a tool for understanding large PRs

extra.author: trezm
extra.original_title: Show HN: Chronosphere, a tool for understanding large PRs

story_text.value:
Hello HN, I wrote a blog post a while back about not sending me your giant PRs (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49305558). Well, I kept getting huge PRs sent to me, so I've been embraced the AI and let it sweep me away.

Chronosphere rebuilds a PR in logical steps to try to recreate the train of thought that went into the generation of the PR itself. It has github and openrouter integrations for convenience, but can also be used entirely from your current coding agent via a skill integration, no code is uploaded to a central server.

Hopefully this helps you all and your battles to understand mass amounts of AI generated code.

title: Gauge
summary: Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs

extra.author: 0x63_Problems
extra.original_title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg

The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop:

- set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks'

- run the tasks

- analyze session transcripts for friction or failures

- create variants of your docs to resolve the issues

- re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname)

- repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues

The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces.

We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product.

The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway.

The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository.

The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys.

The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session.

We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy.

Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior).

The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli

We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli

If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.

We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli

If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.

title: Spooler
summary: a simple, managed message queue

extra.author: gobwas
extra.original_title: Show HN: Spooler – a simple, managed message queue

story_text.value:
Hi Folks,

I'm Sergey, founder of Spooler (https://spooler.sh) -- a durable, fully managed message queue, inspired by the simplicity of Go channels.

Why? Whenever I needed a queue for something, it often felt that adding one would be a bigger project than the solution. Existing systems offered far more than I needed, while using a relational database usually meant inventing queue semantics on the go.

What I really wanted was just a send and recv with retries.

After nearly six months of engineering, I'm really happy to share the result with you.

How it works: you send a message to the queue, you recv it leased; when the message processing is done you acknowledge it, if the lease times out, the message gets back to the queue to be delivered again or into the failed state on too many retries.

There is an atomic ack-and-send: you can acknowledge a message and append another in a single operation. You can model state machines with it: a queue is a state, a message in the queue is an object in that state, and ack-and-send is the transition.

Each Spooler queue lives in a spool: a storage isolation unit (hence the product name) with its own write-ahead log and replication. That means that durable operations succeed only after the log entry is durable on disk and confirmed by the required number of replicas.

Feel free to try it out! There is a docker image for testing it locally: https://docs.spooler.sh/local (it uses the same API but with in-memory storage, which means messages live only as long as the container runs).

Spooler has an open-source CLI and Go library and there is also a repo of agent skills for it. The server itself is closed source, so there is no self-hosted options today.

Please do share your thoughts about the product -- I really hope it feels ordinary to use.

Sergey.

title: Kairos
summary: Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform

extra.author: ayanb9440
extra.original_title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform

story_text.value:
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.

1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.

2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best.

You can self-host Kairos with Docker or use the hosted version at https://kairos.finic.ai

title: vatsaltanna
summary: Scroll from your own skeleton to the edge of the observable universe

extra.author: vatsaltanna
extra.original_title: Show HN: Scroll from your own skeleton to the edge of the observable universe

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I made this to help improve visualisation for a meditation I practise where you picture leaving your body moving outward in stages until you are beyond space-time. It’s helped me get through some really tough times by putting things in perspective.

You start as a skeleton by the pyramids at Giza and scroll past Earth, the planets, the stars, the Milky Way and the galaxy clusters to the edge of the observable universe.

It’s built with real data - 9,096 stars (Yale Bright Star Catalogue), 43,463 galaxies (2MASS Redshift Survey), asteroids (JPL), Earth (NASA Blue Marble) and Giza (Sentinel-2). The cosmic web and the faintest galaxies are generated.

Runs in the browser with three.js and WebGL 2 with no sign-up or tracking. Images are GPU-compressed and load only near their stage which cut peak GPU memory from 1.1 GB to 258 MB.

Hope you have fun playing around and would love to hear what you’d like to see more of!

title: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
summary: AI media manager and video editor

extra.author: lukeigel
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino (https://kino.ai). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video

Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack.

Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match.

Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny.

I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America (https://regressions.net). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet.

Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing.

They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai. We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now.

If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

title: Ask HN
summary: What's your current AI agentic setup?

extra.author: eggbrain
extra.original_title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?

story_text.value:
I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI.

1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc)

- Which tiers?

- Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)?

2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models.

- Which models and providers?

3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses?

- What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)?

4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools?

- For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom.

5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse?

- If you are using them, what are your main use cases?

-----

I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

title: Tell HN
summary: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)

extra.author: jameslk
extra.original_title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)

story_text.value:
If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information.

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988

“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review

“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data

“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”

To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.

I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.

Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424

title: Gitbook Breached
summary: We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could a…

extra.author: punchmesan
extra.original_title: Gitbook Breached

story_text.value:
We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could as it's a mobile paste.

Update:

GitBook security incident update Hey <$name>, The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance.

*What happened* GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data.

*What we did immediately* * Blocked the attacker and closed the vulnerabilities involved * Replaced every credential and secret across our infrastructure * Brought services back only once we were confident they were secure * Invalidated every customer’s API tokens on our platform

*Your data* Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following: * Git Sync secrets. * GitBook API tokens. * Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook. * Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors.

At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified.

*What you need to do now* * Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident. * Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook. * If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets. * If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it. Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process.

*What we are doing next* * Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks. * Introducing further security measures to our platform. * Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident. * If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates

Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption The GitBook team

The strongest sign of a healthy democracy is that people participate in it. It's up to you to decide who to vote for, but no matter who you support, please show up and cast a ballot. A democracy with 75% voter turnout is healthier than a democracy with 50% voter turnout even exactly the same politicians got elected, because citizens participating in a democratic process signals that they value the process and want to keep it.

(Obviously, this only applies to people eligible to vote in ongoing elections. If you're not eligible to vote, please don't vote.)

title: ollama/ollama: v0.40.14
summary:
## What's Changed
* `ollama launch claude` now applies the model's output token limit for Claude Code, so cloud models no longer run into the 128k default cap
* Cloud web search responses on `/api/chat` are now decoded correctly, including compressed responses
* OpenAI-compatible endpoints no longer override a model's packaged sampler defaults — clients that send no `temperature`/`top_p` get the model's own values instead of 1.0, matching `/api/chat`
* `/v1/responses` now preserves readable input content, including prior assistant refusals, instead of flattening it
* Ollama's app can now retry ChatGPT disconnect failures instead of leaving the connection in a broken state
* `ollama launch codex` verifies ChatGPT routing before configuring, and reports a clear error when routing is unavailable
* Faster top-k sampling on MLX for large vocabularies

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.13...v0.40.14

title: ggerganov/llama.cpp: v0.9.0
summary: ## Overview This release adds OCP FP8 E4M3 quantization support, a new `flash_attn_ext_rows` op that makes the unified KV cache efficient for multi-sequence inference, and a generic batched tensor copy API. Four new architectures are supported (Clover, Limite, Metis-1.6 and Mistral Large 4), audio generation and transcription expand with Chatterbox TTS, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and predefined Pocket TTS voices, and the Gemma 4 E2B/E4B models get major prefill optimizations. `ggml` is updated to v0.29.0, bringing FP8 E4M3, flash attention rows, NCCL-based multi-node tensor parallelism and performance work across the CPU, CUDA, SYCL, Metal, Vulkan, OpenCL and Hexagon backends. The server and UI receive a round of fixes and refinements. ### Highlights - Quant: OCP FP8 E4M3 tensor type (saturating mode) with conversion helpers and a new ftype ([#27512](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27512)) - llama: `flash_attn_ext_rows` - more efficient unified KV for multi-seq, restoring non-unified KV prefill performance ([#29510](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29510)) - ggml: batched tensor copy API (`ggml_backend_tensor_copy_n`/`set_n`/`get_n`) superseding the `_2d` API, implemented for Metal and CUDA ([#30881](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30881)) - For a 3rd year in a row, `llama.cpp` is a featured repo in the [Github Octoverse report](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-commits-pushes-reach-new-highs-in-2026-as-developers-build-with-agents/): ### API changes - llama.h: add `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_F8_E4M3` ([#27512](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27512)) - mtmd.h: add `MTMD_GEN_AUDIO_TYPE_CHATTERBOX` and `n_voices` to `mtmd_gen_audio_info` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add predefined-voice APIs: `mtmd_gen_audio_voice_name()`, `mtmd_gen_audio_get_voice()`, `mtmd_gen_state_set_ref()` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add `mtmd_bitmap_is_voice()` and `mtmd_gen_audio_read_tensor()` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add `MTMD_VIDEO_TEMPLATE_QWEN3VL` video prompt template ([#31619](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31619)) - server: `GET /props` reports the model's predefined TTS `voices`; the TTS endpoint accepts predefined voice names ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - server: `/v1/responses` now merges `extra_params` (seed, min_p, ...) into the converted chat-completions response ([#30959](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30959)) ### New models - Clover-35B-A3B-Preview diffusion model, AR mode ([#31306](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31306)) - Limite 1B - Violetto ([#29433](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29433)) - Metis-1.6 (Praxis ~2.9B and Logos ~10.2B): hybrid Mamba-2 / GQA attention with fixed-depth recurrence and LatentMoE ([#31134](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31134)) - Mistral Large 4 ([#31376](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31376)) ### Core changes - gemma4: graph optimizations with massive prefill gains for E2B and E4B ([#31356](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31356)); create `token_embd` before the tied output in gemma3n and gemma4 ([#31394](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31394)) - LFM3: enable NVFP4 GGUFs ([#31608](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31608)), enable tensor split ([#31431](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31431)), quantize the audio codec decoder ([#31386](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31386)) - spec dec: save and restore MTP hidden state in context checkpoints ([#30141](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30141)) and record LFM3 layer inputs ([#31598](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31598)) - dflash: copy hidden features via device copies ([#31506](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31506)); qwen4exp: write the conv state tail without an intermediate cont ([#31443](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31443)) - model loading: reuse the tensor staging buffer and skip the direct-IO bounce buffer ([#31321](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31321)) - kv-cache: keep Hadamard rotation constants on the GPU ([#31073](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31073)) and fix attention tensor rotation in layers with shared KV ([#31406](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31406)) - kv-cache: never return 0 `kv_rows` for sequences without cells ([#31570](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31570)) and refuse rollbacks past the snapshots of the last ubatch ([#31368](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31368)) - Gemma4 MTP assistant: follow `ctx_other` devices and flash-attention setting ([#31635](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31635)); DSV4: remove simple batch splitting ([#31300](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31300)) - chat: strip the qwen3-coder think block with `reasoning_format none` ([#31380](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31380)) and end reasoning budget forcing on a prompt end tag ([#31374](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31374)) - chat: allow a constraint type after the gpt-oss final channel ([#31556](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31556)); common: fix `-hf` tag matching inside longer quant names ([#31620](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31620)) and bound control vector layer indices ([#31336](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31336)) - tools: reject mismatched shards in GGUF split merge ([#31579](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31579)), fix `imatrix --nextn` crash ([#31522](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31522)), fix `gguf-py` `np_roundf` dropping the sign ([#31310](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31310)) - vendor: miniaudio 0.11.26 ([#31459](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31459)) and cpp-httplib 0.64.0 ([#31400](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31400)); embed an app manifest in all Windows executables ([#31329](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31329)) ### Multi-modality changes - add Chatterbox TTS support ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - add Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe support: offline transcription in 40 languages with prompt context and speaker attribution ([#31471](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31471)) - Pocket TTS: support predefined voices without voice cloning ([#31429](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31429)) - accurate support for the qwen3-vl video prompt format ([#31619](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31619)) - resize Gemma 4 images without letterbox padding ([#30922](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30922)) and fix InternVL CLS token order ([#30886](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30886)) ### Server changes - cap shared decision prefixes at the first output ([#30710](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30710)) - restore the speculative checkpoint for drafts longer than `n_rs_seq` ([#31350](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31350)) ### UI changes - add MCP group checkboxes in the tools settings ([#31303](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31303)) and request persistent storage on startup ([#31299](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31299)) - keep chats at the bottom until the reader scrolls up ([#31311](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31311)) and show the submit button when the input has content ([#31324](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31324)) - reveal the collapsed sidebar from its logo ([#31307](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31307)) and align alert dialog styling ([#31312](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31312)) - keep queued steering messages in their own conversation ([#31304](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31304)) and show an interrupted state for tool calls that never returned ([#31314](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31314)) - disable model deletion the server would refuse ([#31305](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31305)) and prefer a loading model in pre-selection ([#31326](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31326)) - add a Playwright harness for recording demo videos ([#31318](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31318)) and run local browser tests in installed Chrome ([#31596](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31596)) ### ggml changes - [v0.29.0](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/releases/tag/v0.29.0): ggml v0.29.0 adds an OCP FP8 E4M3 tensor type, a new `ggml_flash_attn_ext_rows` op where each query slice attends to its own list of K/V rows, a batched tensor copy API, and initial support for multi-node tensor parallelism through a new multi-process communicator interface. Core improvements include bounding tensor views by the bytes their strides reach, zero-copy GGUF export of host-buffer tensors, and `vm_allocate`-based allocations on Apple platforms. Performance work spans all major backends: new SVE kernels in the CPU backend, DPAS flash attention for quantized KV in SYCL, fused MoE MMQ in CUDA, faster MXFP4 mat-vec in Metal, split-K tuning in Vulkan, and a large expansion of quantized GEMM/GEMV coverage in OpenCL. The Hexagon backend gains support for several new ops, including the lightning indexer, top-k mask, conv2d and upscale. ## Assets **Nightly build:** [b12110](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b12110) ## More info - [Releases and versioning of `ggml-org` projects](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/discussions/1579) ## Changelog payload.name: v0.9.0
payload.body: ## Overview This release adds OCP FP8 E4M3 quantization support, a new `flash_attn_ext_rows` op that makes the unified KV cache efficient for multi-sequence inference, and a generic batched tensor copy API. Four new architectures are supported (Clover, Limite, Metis-1.6 and Mistral Large 4), audio generation and transcription expand with Chatterbox TTS, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and predefined Pocket TTS voices, and the Gemma 4 E2B/E4B models get major prefill optimizations. `ggml` is updated to v0.29.0, bringing FP8 E4M3, flash attention rows, NCCL-based multi-node tensor parallelism and performance work across the CPU, CUDA, SYCL, Metal, Vulkan, OpenCL and Hexagon backends. The server and UI receive a round of fixes and refinements. ### Highlights - Quant: OCP FP8 E4M3 tensor type (saturating mode) with conversion helpers and a new ftype ([#27512](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27512)) - llama: `flash_attn_ext_rows` - more efficient unified KV for multi-seq, restoring non-unified KV prefill performance ([#29510](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29510)) - ggml: batched tensor copy API (`ggml_backend_tensor_copy_n`/`set_n`/`get_n`) superseding the `_2d` API, implemented for Metal and CUDA ([#30881](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30881)) - For a 3rd year in a row, `llama.cpp` is a featured repo in the [Github Octoverse report](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-commits-pushes-reach-new-highs-in-2026-as-developers-build-with-agents/): ### API changes - llama.h: add `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_F8_E4M3` ([#27512](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27512)) - mtmd.h: add `MTMD_GEN_AUDIO_TYPE_CHATTERBOX` and `n_voices` to `mtmd_gen_audio_info` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add predefined-voice APIs: `mtmd_gen_audio_voice_name()`, `mtmd_gen_audio_get_voice()`, `mtmd_gen_state_set_ref()` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add `mtmd_bitmap_is_voice()` and `mtmd_gen_audio_read_tensor()` ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - mtmd.h: add `MTMD_VIDEO_TEMPLATE_QWEN3VL` video prompt template ([#31619](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31619)) - server: `GET /props` reports the model's predefined TTS `voices`; the TTS endpoint accepts predefined voice names ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - server: `/v1/responses` now merges `extra_params` (seed, min_p, ...) into the converted chat-completions response ([#30959](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30959)) ### New models - Clover-35B-A3B-Preview diffusion model, AR mode ([#31306](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31306)) - Limite 1B - Violetto ([#29433](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29433)) - Metis-1.6 (Praxis ~2.9B and Logos ~10.2B): hybrid Mamba-2 / GQA attention with fixed-depth recurrence and LatentMoE ([#31134](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31134)) - Mistral Large 4 ([#31376](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31376)) ### Core changes - gemma4: graph optimizations with massive prefill gains for E2B and E4B ([#31356](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31356)); create `token_embd` before the tied output in gemma3n and gemma4 ([#31394](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31394)) - LFM3: enable NVFP4 GGUFs ([#31608](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31608)), enable tensor split ([#31431](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31431)), quantize the audio codec decoder ([#31386](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31386)) - spec dec: save and restore MTP hidden state in context checkpoints ([#30141](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30141)) and record LFM3 layer inputs ([#31598](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31598)) - dflash: copy hidden features via device copies ([#31506](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31506)); qwen4exp: write the conv state tail without an intermediate cont ([#31443](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31443)) - model loading: reuse the tensor staging buffer and skip the direct-IO bounce buffer ([#31321](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31321)) - kv-cache: keep Hadamard rotation constants on the GPU ([#31073](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31073)) and fix attention tensor rotation in layers with shared KV ([#31406](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31406)) - kv-cache: never return 0 `kv_rows` for sequences without cells ([#31570](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31570)) and refuse rollbacks past the snapshots of the last ubatch ([#31368](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31368)) - Gemma4 MTP assistant: follow `ctx_other` devices and flash-attention setting ([#31635](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31635)); DSV4: remove simple batch splitting ([#31300](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31300)) - chat: strip the qwen3-coder think block with `reasoning_format none` ([#31380](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31380)) and end reasoning budget forcing on a prompt end tag ([#31374](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31374)) - chat: allow a constraint type after the gpt-oss final channel ([#31556](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31556)); common: fix `-hf` tag matching inside longer quant names ([#31620](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31620)) and bound control vector layer indices ([#31336](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31336)) - tools: reject mismatched shards in GGUF split merge ([#31579](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31579)), fix `imatrix --nextn` crash ([#31522](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31522)), fix `gguf-py` `np_roundf` dropping the sign ([#31310](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31310)) - vendor: miniaudio 0.11.26 ([#31459](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31459)) and cpp-httplib 0.64.0 ([#31400](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31400)); embed an app manifest in all Windows executables ([#31329](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31329)) ### Multi-modality changes - add Chatterbox TTS support ([#30993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30993)) - add Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe support: offline transcription in 40 languages with prompt context and speaker attribution ([#31471](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31471)) - Pocket TTS: support predefined voices without voice cloning ([#31429](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31429)) - accurate support for the qwen3-vl video prompt format ([#31619](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31619)) - resize Gemma 4 images without letterbox padding ([#30922](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30922)) and fix InternVL CLS token order ([#30886](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30886)) ### Server changes - cap shared decision prefixes at the first output ([#30710](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30710)) - restore the speculative checkpoint for drafts longer than `n_rs_seq` ([#31350](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31350)) ### UI changes - add MCP group checkboxes in the tools settings ([#31303](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31303)) and request persistent storage on startup ([#31299](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31299)) - keep chats at the bottom until the reader scrolls up ([#31311](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31311)) and show the submit button when the input has content ([#31324](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31324)) - reveal the collapsed sidebar from its logo ([#31307](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31307)) and align alert dialog styling ([#31312](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31312)) - keep queued steering messages in their own conversation ([#31304](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31304)) and show an interrupted state for tool calls that never returned ([#31314](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31314)) - disable model deletion the server would refuse ([#31305](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31305)) and prefer a loading model in pre-selection ([#31326](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31326)) - add a Playwright harness for recording demo videos ([#31318](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31318)) and run local browser tests in installed Chrome ([#31596](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31596)) ### ggml changes - [v0.29.0](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/releases/tag/v0.29.0): ggml v0.29.0 adds an OCP FP8 E4M3 tensor type, a new `ggml_flash_attn_ext_rows` op where each query slice attends to its own list of K/V rows, a batched tensor copy API, and initial support for multi-node tensor parallelism through a new multi-process communicator interface. Core improvements include bounding tensor views by the bytes their strides reach, zero-copy GGUF export of host-buffer tensors, and `vm_allocate`-based allocations on Apple platforms. Performance work spans all major backends: new SVE kernels in the CPU backend, DPAS flash attention for quantized KV in SYCL, fused MoE MMQ in CUDA, faster MXFP4 mat-vec in Metal, split-K tuning in Vulkan, and a large expansion of quantized GEMM/GEMV coverage in OpenCL. The Hexagon backend gains support for several new ops, including the lightning indexer, top-k mask, conv2d and upscale. ## Assets **Nightly build:** [b12110](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b12110) ## More info - [Releases and versioning of `ggml-org` projects](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/discussions/1579) ## Changelog
